patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Australia → Fiji: Salesian Julian Fox; Melbourne → Samoa: Salesian priest (alleged); Melbourne → Israel (Malka Leifer flown out by her school); Fort Augustus → Australia: Denis Chrysostom Alexander; New Zealand → Australia: Brother Bernard McGrath; Kevin Lynch: Brisbane Grammar → St Paul's; Ballarat → Sydney: Fr Gerald Ridsdale.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Malka Leifer (Adass Israel School): first report 2008, first action 2021 (13 years). The school flew her to Israel in March 2008 before police were told; Israeli Deputy Health Minister Yaakov Litzman interfered with psychiatric assessments, later pleading guilty to breach of trust; extradition took six years from her 2014 arrest Gerald Ridsdale (Ballarat): first report 1975, first action 1993 (18 years). Bishop Mulkearns knew by 1975 and moved him through parishes; a police officer took the bishop's promise to handle it Frank Houston (Assemblies of God): first report 1999, first action 2015 (16 years). His son Brian Houston, then national president, and the national executive did not refer the 1999 allegations to police
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. The middle of those waits is 12 years. In Rochdale in 1968, a pupil told the police about the local politician Cyril Smith and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role_note: Victoria 2015: Limitation period for child abuse civil claims removed (Feb 2015) New South Wales 2016: Limitation period removed (March 2016) Australian Capital Territory 2016: Limitation period removed (Aug 2016) Northern Territory 2017: Limitation period removed (June 2017) Tasmania 2017: Limitation period removed Western Australia 2018: Limitation period removed (April 2018) South Australia 2018: Limitation period removed (Sept 2018) Queensland 2018: Legislation amended (Nov 2018 per Shine); Queensland first removed the period for institutional child sexual abuse in 2016
patterns.pattern_summary: Most people abused as children do not tell anyone for many years. In many countries and US states the legal deadline for suing or prosecuting, called a statute of limitations, used to run out in a person's early twenties, before most had spoken. When legislatures proposed extending these deadlines or reopening old claims, the institutions that would face lawsuits lobbied against the changes. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million on lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018. In Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference spent more than $7.6 million and the state's insurance federation nearly $20.7 million on lobbying from 2014 to 2024. These totals cover all the issues they lobbied on, not only this one. Where the deadlines were lifted anyway, many institutions filed for bankruptcy. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders did so, several of them hours or days before a trial, a deposition or a new law took effect. The Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics also filed.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 1999: Commission of Inquiry into Abuse of Children in Queensland Institutions (Forde Inquiry), 1999. Found abuse had occurred; 42 recommendations
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. The research for this map found no national inquiry in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Malka Leifer: Extradited January 2021; convicted 3 April 2023; Litzman took a plea deal for breach of trust and resigned from the Knesset (2022)
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 1 documented adoption flows into Australia on this map.
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: Vietnam — Operation Babylift (1975): not all children were orphans (receiving or involved). Australia — Stolen Generations: Bringing Them Home (1997) and national apology (2008). Australia — forced adoptions: Senate inquiry 2012 and national apology 2013.
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, about 500 babies were taken from mothers held in detention and given to other families; in 2012 a court found this had been a "systematic plan", and by July 2025, 140 of those children had been identified. Under Franco's dictatorship in Spain, children were taken from Republican mothers and later from unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children from their families and placed them in residential schools or with non-Indigenous families. In 1951 Denmark sent a group of Greenlandic children to live with Danish families, and France moved children from the island of Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported children from occupied parts of Ukraine; in March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over these deportations.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 1994: Crimes (Child Sex Tourism) Amendment Act 1994 in force 5 July 1994 — one of the first offender-country laws 2017: Australia: laws from 13 Dec 2017 allow cancelling passports of up to 20,000 registered child sex offenders; about 800 registered offenders had travelled abroad the previous year
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role: Police ran abuse sites to catch users
patterns.role_note: Queensland Police Task Force Argos ran the Childs Play site for about 11 months (2016–17).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect networks that abuse children circulate widely. The records gathered for this map show a few cases where a state service was involved, several claims that investigations found to be false, and some that remain unproven. In Chile, Paul Schäfer, who founded the German settlement Colonia Dignidad in 1961, was convicted in 2006 of abusing children there; Chilean officials believe the Pinochet dictatorship used the settlement to torture its opponents, and Germany admitted in 2016 that its embassy had failed to act. In West Berlin, from the late 1960s, the city's youth authorities placed boys in foster care with men known to be paedophiles, on the advice of the psychologist Helmut Kentler. In Afghanistan, US soldiers were told not to intervene when Afghan commanders allied with them abused boys. In Bosnia around 2001, UN police monitors and employees of a US contractor bought women and girls who had been trafficked. In the United States and Australia, police took over websites used to share abuse images and kept them running for weeks or months to identify the users. Investigations found no evidence that MI5 used the Kincora boys' home in Belfast for blackmail, and the ring of powerful men that London police investigated in Operation Midland was invented by Carl Beech, who was later jailed. The claim that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency has not been established.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role_note: Australia → Philippines payments for livestreamed abuse.
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Australia — forced adoptions: Senate inquiry 2012 and national apology 2013; Australia — Stolen Generations: Bringing Them Home (1997) and national apology (2008); Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse — final report; Parramatta Training School for Girls and Hay Institution — Royal Commission Case Study 7; Bringing Them Home — Stolen Generations inquiry; Forde Inquiry — abuse of children in Queensland institutions; Mullighan Inquiry — Children in State Care, South Australia; Royal Commission into the Protection and Detention of Children in the Northern Territory (Don Dale); Tasmanian Commission of Inquiry — Ashley Youth Detention Centre, Launceston General Hospital, schools and out-of-home care; Brisbane Grammar / St Paul's — counsellor abuse; Governor-General resigns over church handling; Royal Commission Case Study 36 — Church of England Boys' Society; Dio.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 238 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: South Korea — Brothers Home children sent overseas for adoption
cases.who: Brothers Home (Busan detention facility); receiving agencies named by AP incl. Holt International, Children's Home Society of Minnesota
cases.what: Brothers Home was a state-backed facility where people deemed vagrants were confined and forced to work; the TRC recognised state culpability on 23 August 2022 and counted 657 deaths there 1975–1988. An AP investigation (November 2019) found Brothers Home organised the adoption of 19 children abroad in 1979–1986 and that six US agencies received children from it. In February 2025 the TRC confirmed at least 31 children were improperly sent overseas for adoption through the facility.

cases.title: British child migration programmes — IICSA
cases.who: UK government; Fairbridge Society, Barnardo's, Sisters of Nazareth, Catholic Church agencies and others; receiving institutions incl. Christian Brothers
cases.what: IICSA's report of 1 March 2018 found that the child migration programmes were 'a deeply flawed government policy' and that successive UK governments failed to ensure protections against abuse. It found a catalogue of evidence that migrated children suffered ill-treatment and abuse including sexual abuse; Barnardo's suspended migration after sexual abuse came to light at its Picton school, and the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to allegations at its schools in Canada and Australia. It recommended an immediate financial redress scheme for surviving child migrants.
cases.cover_up: Successive governments continued the policy despite years of evidence that children were suffering, including sexual abuse. Fairbridge failed to respond properly to a series of sexual abuse allegations at its schools.

cases.title: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse — final report
cases.who: Religious, government and other institutions; evidence related to 3,489 institutions
cases.what: The Royal Commission, announced in November 2012, delivered its final report on 15 December 2017 with a total of 409 recommendations across its reports. It held 8,013 private sessions, received 1,344 written accounts and heard evidence relating to 3,489 institutions. 58.1% of survivors in private sessions reported abuse in a religious institution, 32.5% in a government-run institution and 10.5% in other non-government institutions. The average age at first abuse was 10.4 years. Its recommendations led to the National Redress Scheme, which began on 1 July 2018.
cases.cover_up: Case studies documented destroyed or unkept records and the protection of institutional reputation over children, e.g. the Catholic Diocese of Ballarat ('records were deliberately not made or kept or were destroyed').

cases.title: Parramatta Training School for Girls and Hay Institution — Royal Commission Case Study 7
cases.who: NSW state child-welfare department; Parramatta Girls Home (Parramatta Training School for Girls), Hay Institution for Girls
cases.what: Parramatta Girls Home was a NSW state-run institution for girls from 1887 to 1974, many of them Aboriginal girls of the Stolen Generations. The Royal Commission's February 2014 hearing (Case Study 7, report October 2014) heard evidence about 11 men, most of them superintendents or deputies, accused of physical and sexual abuse. Most alleged perpetrators were never reported or investigated and no criminal charges were laid. A 2004 Senate inquiry had earlier taken statements from 20 former residents.
cases.cover_up: Most alleged perpetrators were never reported or investigated; some resigned or were dismissed after inquiries; no criminal charges were laid.

cases.title: Forde Inquiry — abuse of children in Queensland institutions
cases.who: 159 government and non-government orphanages, reformatories and detention centres in Queensland
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Abuse of Children in Queensland Institutions, chaired by former governor Leneen Forde, was set up on 13 August 1998 and reported in May 1999. It examined 159 institutions from 1911 to 1999, found that abuse had occurred and made 42 recommendations. Some findings were sealed because matters were still before the courts. It led to state apologies, the Queensland Government Redress Scheme and the Forde Foundation.

cases.title: Mullighan Inquiry — Children in State Care, South Australia
cases.who: South Australian state guardianship system (Families SA and predecessors)
cases.what: Commissioner Ted Mullighan's inquiry began in November 2004 and was widened in 2007 to children on the Anangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara (APY) Lands. Its March 2008 report found 'that in the past 65 years the State has failed to protect some of the children in its care from sexual abuse' and that record-keeping on 924 children who died in state care was manifestly inadequate. It made 54 recommendations, and 400 suspected abusers were reported to South Australia Police.

cases.title: Royal Commission into the Protection and Detention of Children in the Northern Territory (Don Dale)
cases.who: Northern Territory Government youth detention and child protection systems
cases.what: The Royal Commission into the Protection and Detention of Children in the Northern Territory was set up in July 2016 after ABC Four Corners broadcast footage of boys at Don Dale being tear-gassed, hooded with spit hoods and shackled. Its final report, released on 17 November 2017 by commissioners Margaret White and Mick Gooda, found children had been subjected to 'regular, repeated and distressing mistreatment in detention' and that the law was often not followed, and recommended closing Don Dale, raising the age of criminal responsibility to 12 and not detaining children under 14.
cases.cover_up: A 2014 media release falsely said six boys had escaped when CCTV showed one; two earlier reports (January 2015 review and the August 2015 Children's Commissioner report) were not acted on.

cases.title: Tasmanian Commission of Inquiry — Ashley Youth Detention Centre, Launceston General Hospital, schools and out-of-home care
cases.who: Tasmanian Government: Ashley Youth Detention Centre, Launceston General Hospital paediatric ward, public schools, Child Safety Services, Tasmania Police
cases.what: The commission, called in 2020 after a podcast aired allegations against Launceston General Hospital paediatric nurse James Griffin (who died in 2019 after being charged with child sexual offences), released a 3,500-page final report in 2023 with 75 findings and 191 recommendations. It found the state's response to child sexual abuse since 2000 had too often been inadequate, sometimes to protect reputations. Children at Ashley Youth Detention Centre had experienced systematic harm and abuse for decades and sexual abuse remained a 'live and current' risk; the commission repeated its call for Ashley to close. Premier Jeremy Rockliff apologised in parliament.
cases.cover_up: Launceston General Hospital failed to act on a 2011 or 2012 disclosure about nurse James Griffin, leaving children at risk for eight years; Tasmania Police failed to act on 'highly probative' evidence from the Australian Federal Police in 2015; the government had been on notice about unlawful isolation at Ashley since at least 2013.

cases.title: Brisbane Grammar / St Paul's — counsellor abuse; Governor-General resigns over church handling
cases.who: Brisbane Grammar School; St Paul's School; Anglican Diocese of Brisbane (Archbishop Peter Hollingworth)
cases.what: School counsellor Kevin John Lynch, who worked at Brisbane Grammar and then at the Anglican St Paul's School in the 1980s and 1990s, abused students; music teacher Gregory Knight at St Paul's was a convicted paedophile. Peter Hollingworth was Anglican Archbishop of Brisbane from 1989 to 2001. An Anglican church inquiry report, tabled in the Queensland parliament on 1 May 2003, found he had acted unfairly in some cases, notably in allowing a known paedophile to continue as a priest; he resigned as Governor-General on 25 May 2003. In November 2015 the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse examined the two schools' handling of the abuse, and Hollingworth apologised to victims.
cases.cover_up: Brisbane Grammar quietly investigated complaints about counsellor Kevin Lynch in the early 1980s; he moved to St Paul's. A 2003 diocesan inquiry found Archbishop Hollingworth in 1993 allowed a known abuser to keep working as a priest.

cases.title: Royal Commission Case Study 36 — Church of England Boys' Society
cases.who: Church of England Boys' Society (now Anglican Boys' Society / Boys' Ministry Australia); Anglican dioceses of Sydney, Brisbane, Adelaide and Tasmania
cases.what: The Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse reported in February 2017 that the CEBS youth group gave paedophiles easy access to boys from the 1970s to the 1990s, with abuse on camps, sailing and fishing trips and overnight stays at rectories. It found 'networks of sexual perpetrators at CEBS who had knowledge of each other's sexual offending against boys and in some instances facilitated' it; several associated men were later convicted. It found a focus on protecting the reputation of the church, dioceses, CEBS and clergy.
cases.cover_up: Allegations were not reported to police at all or not in time; a parish priest told one victim to 'let sleeping dogs lie'. The report found Peter Hollingworth, former Archbishop of Brisbane and later Governor-General, made 'a serious error of judgment' in letting an accused priest continue in ministry.

cases.title: Anglican Diocese of Brisbane — Archbishop Peter Hollingworth's handling of abuse
cases.who: Anglican Diocese of Brisbane; Toowoomba Preparatory School; Church of England Boys' Society
cases.what: Peter Hollingworth was Anglican Archbishop of Brisbane from 1989 to 2001 and became Governor-General in June 2001. In December 2001 he faced allegations that he had handled sexual abuse cases poorly as archbishop. His successor, Phillip Aspinall, set up a church inquiry in February 2002 into the handling of nine abuse cases; its report was tabled in the Queensland Parliament on 1 May 2003, and Aspinall said Hollingworth had made a 'grave and serious' error of judgement. Hollingworth announced his resignation as Governor-General on 25 May 2003.
cases.cover_up: A diocesan inquiry found that in 1993 Archbishop Hollingworth allowed a known paedophile to keep working as a priest. He later became Governor-General of Australia.

cases.title: Childs Play — run by Australia's Task Force Argos for 11 months
cases.who: Childs Play (Tor forum; owner Benjamin Faulkner, convicted)
cases.what: Childs Play launched on Tor on 15 April 2016 and, with over a million registered profiles, was described as the largest site of its kind. Its Canadian administrator, Benjamin Faulkner, was arrested in Virginia in early October 2016 with American Patrick Falte; in September 2017 a federal judge in Virginia sentenced both to life for sexually abusing a toddler, and in August 2019 both received 35 years for running a child exploitation enterprise on the related Giftbox Exchange site. Australia's Task Force Argos then ran Childs Play for 11 months, until September 2017, as part of Operation Artemis, to identify victims and offenders.
cases.cover_up: Queensland Police Task Force Argos operated the site for about 11 months (2016–2017), impersonating the owner and posting abuse images to keep users' trust; a UNICEF Norway legal adviser and Amnesty International criticised this, ECPAT supported it, and a York University criminologist called the server move to Australia 'jurisdiction shopping'.

cases.title: Landslide Productions / Operations Avalanche and Ore
cases.who: Landslide Productions (payment portal, Thomas and Janice Reedy)
cases.what: Landslide, a Fort Worth, Texas portal run by Thomas and Janice Reedy, processed credit-card sign-ups for third-party sites, some offering child abuse images. US agents raided it in August 1999; a jury convicted Thomas Reedy, who was sentenced to 1,335 years (reduced to 180 on appeal), and Janice Reedy got 14 years. US Operation Avalanche examined about 35,000 names on the database, and the FBI passed details of 7,272 British residents to UK police, starting Operation Ore, Britain's biggest computer crime investigation; raids began in May 2002. CEOP said 140 children had been rescued in the UK. Later forensic examination showed large-scale credit card fraud in Landslide's records (54,348 sets of stolen card details), and some people were wrongly accused; a legal challenge in 2009 argued that many convictions for incitement rested on flawed credit-card evidence. Follow-on operations took place in other countries.
cases.cover_up: Later reconstruction of the Landslide data found many listed names were victims of credit-card fraud, and the validity of UK Operation Ore procedures was questioned; an estimated 33 suicides followed in the UK.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Diocese of Ballarat — Gerald Ridsdale and Royal Commission Case Study 28
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Ballarat; Bishop Ronald Mulkearns
cases.what: Gerald Ridsdale, ordained 1961, was convicted in a series of trials from 1993 of abusing more than 70 children; he died in prison in 2025. He was moved between parishes including Mildura, Swan Hill, Warrnambool, Apollo Bay, Edenhope and Mortlake, then to Sydney. The Royal Commission's Ballarat report of 6 December 2017 found Bishop Mulkearns knew of his offending by late 1975 and still reappointed him, a 'catastrophic' failure. It also found police obstruction of a 1972 investigation of Monsignor John Day.
cases.cover_up: Ridsdale moved through about 13 postings 1962–1991; Mulkearns knew by late 1975; a senior police officer in 1972 offered a detective promotion to stop investigating Monsignor John Day

flows.title: Seoul → Australia
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Australia; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: Saigon → Australia (removal)
flows.what: Operation Babylift children sent to Australia.

flows.title: UK → Australia child migrants
flows.what: Children in British care were sent to institutions in Australia where IICSA found a catalogue of evidence of ill-treatment and sexual abuse; the last child was migrated in 1970.

flows.title: Kevin Lynch: Brisbane Grammar → St Paul's
flows.what: After complaints were quietly investigated at Brisbane Grammar in the early 1980s, counsellor Kevin Lynch later worked at St Paul's School, where he also abused students; he was charged in 1997.

flows.what: AUSTRAC alleged Westpac failed to vet transactions that could be linked to child exploitation and live child sex shows in the Philippines (A$1.3bn penalty, 2020); an Australian man paid a Filipino mother while directing abuse over Skype for nearly five years. IJM's 2020 study ranked Australians third among purchasers.

flows.title: Australian offender relocates to the Philippines
flows.what: Peter Scully fled Melbourne for the Philippines in 2011 and ran a pay-per-view abuse site there; life sentence 2018.

flows.title: Australia → Philippines travelling offenders
flows.what: Several Australian men have been convicted in Australia for abusing children in the Philippines, including a flight attendant who abused 26 girls from 2010 to 2017.

flows.title: Australia → Southeast Asia registered offenders' travel
flows.what: Australia's Foreign Minister said about 800 registered child sex offenders travelled abroad in 2016, often to developing countries in Asia, with 40% not notifying police.

flows.title: Fort Augustus → Australia: Denis Chrysostom Alexander
flows.what: After a pupil's parents complained, the abbey school sent the monk back to Australia without telling police; he was arrested in Sydney in 2017 and pleaded guilty in 2021.

flows.title: Australia → Fiji: Salesian Julian Fox
flows.what: Fox was transferred to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating him; he was jailed in 2015.

networks.name: South Korea's four authorised overseas adoption agencies (Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
networks.what: The four agencies held guardianship over children and sent them abroad under government policy; Holt sent about half (AP). The TRC (March 2025) found agencies met monthly quotas for foreign partners, falsified orphan status and swapped identities, and that the state failed to supervise them. All four were implicated in the petitions (Guardian, 2023).

networks.name: British child migration programmes
networks.what: UK government-backed schemes run by Barnardo's, the Fairbridge Society, Catholic agencies and others that sent children to Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Southern Rhodesia; IICSA found sexual abuse and failure to protect.

networks.name: Orphanage trafficking and orphanage tourism (recruitment of children into institutions for donations)
networks.what: A recurring pattern in which orphanages are set up or kept full to attract foreign donations, volunteers and tourists, recruiting children who mostly have living parents, sometimes with payments to families or forged documents. Governments and the US State Department have recognised it as trafficking, and Australia's parliament classed it as modern slavery in 2017.

networks.name: Boylover forum

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: New Zealand → Australia: Brother Bernard McGrath; New Zealand → Papua New Guinea: priests sent after allegations; Australia / New Zealand → Fiji: transferred clergy.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2018: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care, 2018 - final report 24 July 2024. Between 113,000 and 253,000 children, young people and adults abused and neglected in care 1950-1999
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. The research for this map found no national inquiry in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 1 documented adoption flows into New Zealand on this map.
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: British child migration programmes — IICSA (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, about 500 babies were taken from mothers held in detention and given to other families; in 2012 a court found this had been a "systematic plan", and by July 2025, 140 of those children had been identified. patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 2005: New Zealand Crimes Amendment Act 2005 criminalises sexual conduct with children abroad by citizens and residents
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Lake Alice Hospital Child and Adolescent Unit — torture finding; Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care — 'Whanaketia' final report.

cases.title: British child migration programmes — IICSA
cases.who: UK government; Fairbridge Society, Barnardo's, Sisters of Nazareth, Catholic Church agencies and others; receiving institutions incl. Christian Brothers
cases.what: IICSA's report of 1 March 2018 found that the child migration programmes were 'a deeply flawed government policy' and that successive UK governments failed to ensure protections against abuse. It found a catalogue of evidence that migrated children suffered ill-treatment and abuse including sexual abuse; Barnardo's suspended migration after sexual abuse came to light at its Picton school, and the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to allegations at its schools in Canada and Australia. It recommended an immediate financial redress scheme for surviving child migrants.
cases.cover_up: Successive governments continued the policy despite years of evidence that children were suffering, including sexual abuse. Fairbridge failed to respond properly to a series of sexual abuse allegations at its schools.

cases.title: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care — 'Whanaketia' final report
cases.who: State social welfare, disability, mental health, education, law-enforcement and faith-based care settings
cases.what: The final report, made public on 24 July 2024, found abuse was rife in state and faith-based care and that sexual abuse was commonplace, with abusers grooming people in care. It estimated 200,000 of about 655,000 people in care between 1950 and 2019 were abused; Māori were more likely to be abused. Commissioners Coral Shaw, Andrew Erueti and Paul Gibson made 138 recommendations, including a specialist investigation unit and an independent Care Safe Agency, and called it 'a national disgrace'.
cases.cover_up: Commissioners found the state failed to respond to signs of systemic abuse and neglect, and that by 2024 there had been very little progress on the redress system they recommended in 2021.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Lake Alice Hospital Child and Adolescent Unit — torture finding
cases.who: Lake Alice state psychiatric hospital, child and adolescent unit; psychiatrist Selwyn Leeks
cases.what: Between 1972 and 1978, 362 children went through the child and adolescent unit at Lake Alice state psychiatric hospital; about half were Māori boys. Survivors described electric shocks without anaesthetic and painful paraldehyde injections used as punishment, and evidence was given of children being raped and sexually abused by staff and adult patients. In 2019 the UN Committee Against Torture found New Zealand had breached the Convention by failing to investigate properly; police opened a new investigation in 2020. Psychiatrist Selwyn Leeks denied abuse and was never criminally charged in New Zealand. The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care found many of the children were tortured, and on 18 Dec 2024 the government announced NZ$150,000 redress per survivor and a new Crown apology explicitly acknowledging torture.
cases.cover_up: The Crown's internal policy refused to recognise the long-term effects of abuse, forcing complaints to the UN Committee Against Torture in 2019.

cases.title: Royal Commission into Abuse in Care — Catholic institutions
cases.who: Catholic Church in Aotearoa New Zealand; St John of God Brothers at Marylands School
cases.what: The Royal Commission's final report, Whanaketia, published 24 July 2024, found about 200,000 people were abused in state and faith-based care from 1950 to 2019. It found Catholic responses inadequate, noting a 2020 church briefing that 14% of clergy were accused over 1950–1999, and singled out Marylands School in Christchurch for some of the highest levels of sexual abuse. It found abusers were transferred to other ministries and recommended an inquiry into priests sent to Papua New Guinea.
cases.cover_up: Church relied on psychiatrists' opinions to transfer abusers to other ministries where they reoffended; commission recommended investigating priests transferred to Papua New Guinea

cases.title: Marylands School and Hebron Trust — St John of God Brothers
cases.who: Brothers Hospitallers of St John of God
cases.what: Marylands, a Christchurch residential school for boys with learning disabilities run by the St John of God Brothers, and the order's later Hebron Trust were described by survivors to the Royal Commission as 'hell on earth'. Its August 2023 report found widespread sexual and physical abuse: more than one in five of the 537 boys who attended Marylands reported abuse between 1955 and 1984, and 21 of the 37 Brothers who served at Marylands and in Christchurch faced abuse allegations. At Hebron Trust youths were abused by Brother Bernard McGrath, who has been convicted of more than 100 offences in New Zealand and Australia.
cases.cover_up: Brother Bernard McGrath was transferred to Australia after 1977 allegations and later put in charge of Hebron Trust; victims sometimes required to sign non-disclosure agreements
cases.network: Brothers Hospitallers of St John of God

cases.title: Frank Houston — Royal Commission Case Study 18 (Assemblies of God / Hillsong)
cases.who: Assemblies of God in Australia (now Australian Christian Churches); Hillsong Church
cases.what: Pastor Frank Houston sexually abused a young boy in the 1970s. The Royal Commission's Case Study 18 findings (November 2015) found that Brian Houston and the national executive did not report the allegations to police when they emerged in 1999, and that Brian Houston had a conflict of interest as both national president and the son of the alleged perpetrator. Frank Houston died in 2004 without being charged.
cases.cover_up: When allegations surfaced in 1999, Brian Houston, then National President of the Assemblies of God and Frank Houston's son, confronted his father, who confessed; Brian Houston and the National Executive did not refer the matter to police.
cases.network: Hillsong Church / Australian Christian Churches (Assemblies of God)

cases.title: 764 network — founder sentenced to 80 years
cases.who: 764 (online network on Discord/Telegram; founder Bradley Cadenhead)
cases.what: 764, named after the first digits of the ZIP code of Stephenville, Texas, extorted minors into producing abuse material, self-harm and animal cruelty. Its founder, Bradley Cadenhead, was arrested in August 2021 aged 16 and on 16 May 2023 was sentenced in Texas to 80 years after pleading guilty to nine counts of possession/promotion of child sexual abuse material. The US DOJ describes 764 as a nihilistic violent extremist network and its Counterterrorism Section prosecutes it; on 29 April 2025 DOJ announced the arrests of two alleged leaders of the subgroup '764 Inferno', in North Carolina and in Greece. On 10 December 2025 Canada became the first country to list 764 as a terrorist entity.

cases.title: Operation Blackwrist — Thai boys abused for Tor sites
cases.who: Tor site administrators in Thailand and Australia
cases.what: INTERPOL launched Operation Blackwrist in 2017 after finding, during routine dark web monitoring, material showing the abuse of 11 boys under 13, published weekly on a subscription website with nearly 63,000 users. Bulgaria's cybercrime police, supported by Europol, took down the servers; US HSI, New Zealand's Department of Internal Affairs, NCMEC and Australian police assisted. The main administrator in Thailand and a second administrator in Adelaide, Australia, were arrested in January 2018. In June 2018 a Thai court sentenced the Thai administrator to 146 years, and an associate received 36 years; on 17 May 2019 the Australian administrator was sentenced to 40 years and three months, the longest sentence ever imposed in Australia for child sex offences. INTERPOL said 50 children had been removed from harm and 9 offenders arrested in Thailand, Australia and the United States.

cases.title: Matthew Falder — dark web 'hurtcore' blackmailer
cases.who: Individual offender posting on hurtcore dark web sites
cases.what: A Cambridge-educated Birmingham university researcher posed online as a depressed female artist to lure victims, some as young as 14, into sending images, then blackmailed them into sending increasingly degrading material, which he shared on dark web 'hurtcore' sites. The NCA estimated more than 50 victims between 2009 and 2017. A taskforce of the NCA, GCHQ, US Homeland Security Investigations, the Australian Federal Police and Europol, with police in Israel and Slovenia, identified him after four years; he was arrested in June 2017. He admitted 137 of 188 charges and was jailed for 32 years in February 2018, thought to be the first UK prosecution related to hurtcore material; in October 2018 the Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to 25 years.
cases.cover_up: The NCA said technology companies' limited cooperation may have delayed identifying victims.

cases.title: Marist Brothers and priests — New Zealand convictions
cases.who: Marist Brothers; Society of Mary
cases.what: A 2018 Otago Daily Times report listed nine Marist Brothers convicted of crimes against boys in New Zealand, including two at Hato Paora College. Marist priest Alan Woodcock was extradited from England and convicted in 2004 of 21 offences (1978–1987). Brother Kevin Healy was convicted in 2020. The church admitted in 2022 that 14% of its diocesan clergy had been accused since 1950.

cases.title: Fiji — transferred clergy and Julian Fox
cases.who: Salesians; Catholic Church in Fiji
cases.what: Salesian priest Julian Fox was moved to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating abuse allegations; he was jailed in Australia in 2015. The Catholic Church in Fiji knew of the allegations nine years before he was charged. In July 2020 1News reported that some of about 1,300 alleged child abuse cases involving clergy in Fiji concerned clergy from Australia and New Zealand.
cases.cover_up: Fox was transferred to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating; the Fiji church knew of allegations nine years before he was charged

cases.title: Dilworth School — Anglican boarding school, Auckland
cases.who: Dilworth Trust (Anglican-linked school for boys from disadvantaged families)
cases.what: Police arrested and charged six men on 14 September 2020 over offences at Dilworth alleged to date from the 1970s to the early 2000s. An independent inquiry led by Dame Silvia Cartwright and Frances Joychild KC, released on 18 September 2023 and covering 1950 to the present, found that sexual abuse was committed consistently from the mid-1950s to the end of 2005: 126 of 171 former students who gave information reported being sexually abused, and the inquiry knew of 49 more. Police estimated 233 student victims. The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care also examined Dilworth.
cases.cover_up: The independent inquiry concluded that ongoing silence about the abuse was 'the primary reason for the damage' to former students.

cases.title: Gloriavale Christian Community — convictions and Employment Court findings
cases.who: Gloriavale Christian Community
cases.what: Founder Neville Cooper ('Hopeful Christian') was sentenced in December 1995 to five years in prison on three charges of indecent assault against a young woman, after an earlier conviction on 10 counts involving five young complainants was overturned on appeal. In May 2022 the Employment Court ruled that three former members had been employees from age six, doing 'strenuous, difficult and sometimes dangerous' work. Leader Howard Temple pleaded guilty in 2025 to indecently assaulting six girls and young women between 2002 and 2022, resigned as leader, and on 12 December 2025 was jailed for 26 months.
cases.cover_up: In January 2025 Gloriavale's leadership said past leaders had not reported known abuse to authorities; in 2026 the Charities Registration Board cited the school's failure to report child sexual offending.

cases.title: Operation Rescue — Boylover forum network
cases.who: Boylover forum (Netherlands-hosted)
cases.what: A forum presenting itself as 'discussion-only' where members made contact before moving to private channels to share abuse images. UK CEOP traced the owner and the server to the Netherlands in 2009; Europol rebuilt the forum offline and sent 4,202 intelligence reports to 25 EU states and 8 other countries. By March 2011, 670 suspects had been identified, 184 arrested and 230 children safeguarded, which Europol called the highest number for such an investigation.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

In January 2011 families of 261 babies who disappeared from Spanish hospitals over five decades asked the attorney general to investigate an alleged network of doctors and nurses; lawyers claimed up to 300,000 babies were taken.
