Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Morocco — royal pardon of Spanish child rapist Daniel Galván (2013)
cases.who: Daniel Galván Viña
cases.what: Daniel Galván Viña, a retired Spanish professor, was arrested in Morocco in December 2010 and in September 2011 sentenced to 30 years for raping 11 Moroccan children aged 4 to 14. In late July 2013 he was among 48 Spanish prisoners pardoned by King Mohammed VI; after protests outside parliament in Rabat, the king revoked the pardon on 4 August 2013, citing the gravity of the crimes and the victims' rights, and said he had not been told the details of the case. Galván had already left Morocco; he was later arrested in Spain.
cases.cover_up: King Mohammed VI pardoned Galván on 30 July 2013 among 48 Spanish prisoners; he left Morocco on an expired passport with authorities' knowledge before the pardon was cancelled. Protesters in Rabat were violently dispersed. A 2010 US cable reported a 2006 royal pardon of a French man convicted of abusing a 15-year-old boy in Marrakesh.

cases.title: Romania — post-1989 adoption trade and 2004 ban
cases.who: Private adoption agencies and intermediaries; Romanian authorities
cases.what: After Ceaușescu's fall, television images of about 100,000 children in orphanages led to an adoption boom; private agencies charged €7,500–25,000 and the system 'quickly became awash in corruption' (DW). Romania halted adoptions in June 1991 and, under EU pressure, passed a law in June 2004 banning all foreign adoptions except by grandparents. The European Parliament's rapporteur Baroness Emma Nicholson had criticised 'international adoption and child trafficking' in Romania. Romania's own HCCH return shows 458 intercountry adoptions in 2002, 332 in 2003, 2 in 2005 and 0 in 2006.

cases.title: China — intercountry adoption programme ended (2024) after trafficking cases
cases.who: China Center for Children's Welfare and Adoption; state orphanages
cases.what: China opened intercountry adoption in 1992; about 160,000 children were sent abroad, peaking at almost 8,000 to the US in 2005. The programme came to depend increasingly on abuse, abduction and trafficking (New Yorker), including Hunan orphanages buying trafficked babies (2005). On 5 September 2024 the foreign ministry announced the end of the programme, except adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.

cases.title: Nigeria — cult-linked networks traffic women and girls to Europe and West African mines (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Nigerian organized trafficking networks, some linked to cult organizations/confraternities
cases.what: The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report says highly organized groups, sometimes linked to Nigerian cult organizations or confraternities, recruit and exploit Nigerian women and girls in sex trafficking in Italy, Spain and the UK, and that networks move women and girls to mining regions in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire. In the reporting year courts convicted 49 traffickers and the government identified 2,058 victims. It describes corruption and official complicity, including among officials responsible for anti-trafficking, as significant concerns.

cases.title: Romania — girls in state institutions at risk; victims sent across Europe (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers; staff of some government-run institutions
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says most identified victims are women and girls exploited in Romania and in Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK; children in government-run institutions, particularly girls in homes for persons with disabilities, are at risk of sex trafficking; and Roma children as young as 11 are 'sold' into marriage. Courts convicted 161 traffickers (143 for sex trafficking) and 600 victims were identified in 2024.
cases.cover_up: Alleged complicity, misconduct and negligence by government employees in cases involving children in government-run homes remained a concern.

cases.title: Spanish Ombudsman report on Church abuse
cases.who: Catholic Church in Spain
cases.what: Spain's first official inquiry into clergy abuse, a nearly 800-page report by Ombudsman Ángel Gabilondo presented to parliament on 27 October 2023 after an 18-month investigation of 487 cases, criticised the church's response as often minimising or denying the problem. A GAD3 survey of 8,000 adults in the report found 1.13% said they had been abused as children by clergy or lay church members and 0.6% by clergy. Gabilondo did not extrapolate a victim count; media applying the percentages to Spain's adult population put the figure at about 440,000 (or about 200,000 for clergy alone). The Spanish bishops apologised but disputed the media figures.

cases.title: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
cases.who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cases.what: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
cases.cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.

cases.title: Regpay — Minsk-based paid abuse sites / Operation Falcon
cases.who: Regpay Co. Ltd (Belarus) with Florida payment firm Connections
cases.what: Regpay Co. Ltd of Minsk, Belarus, processed paid memberships to about 50 websites, including child abuse sites it operated itself, serving thousands of subscribers worldwide; payments were laundered with help from Connections USA of Fort Lauderdale, Florida. US Attorney General John Ashcroft announced the case in January 2004 as part of Operation Falcon. Regpay's president Yahor Zalatarou and marketing director Alexei Buchnev were arrested at a Paris hotel on 30 July 2003 after a ruse by US agents, and technical administrator Aliaksandr Boika was arrested in Tarragona, Spain, on 31 July 2003 and extradited. All pleaded guilty in New Jersey. Buchnev was sentenced to 40 months in May 2006; Zalatarou and Boika were each sentenced to 25 years on 9 August 2006. Connections' chief executive pleaded guilty to money laundering. Hundreds of subscribers were arrested in the US and other countries.

cases.title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
cases.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
cases.what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

cases.title: Marcial Maciel and the Legion of Christ — 2019 internal report
cases.who: Legion of Christ (Legionaries); founder Marcial Maciel
cases.what: For decades until 2006 the Vatican dismissed accusations by seminarians that founder Marcial Maciel had abused them. In 2006 it ordered him to retire to a life of 'prayer and penitence', and on 1 May 2010, after an apostolic visitation, it said his acts were 'true crimes'. The Legion's own report, released on 21 December 2019, found that 175 minors were abused by 33 of its priests between 1941 and 2019; at least 60 of them by Maciel. It said 111 of the 175 were victims of Maciel or of his victims, and that 14 of the 33 abusive priests had themselves been abused within the order.
cases.cover_up: Letters to the Vatican in 1976, 1978 and 1989 and formal charges in 1998 produced no action; Vatican in 2010 said the Legion had shielded Maciel; Maciel never laicised or tried

cases.title: Operation Atlantic — FBI and EU follow-up to Boylover network
cases.who: Online offender networks incl. members of the Boylover network
cases.what: A joint FBI–EU investigation coordinated by Europol from November 2010. By February 2012, 37 child sex offenders had been identified and 17 arrested for molestation and production of illegal content; 8 victims were identified. Two targets had been members of the Boylover network tackled in Operation Rescue.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

flows.title: Bucharest → Spain
flows.what: Romanian intercountry adoptions to Spain in 2002, during the moratorium period before the 2004 ban.

flows.title: Europe → Tangier, Morocco (tourist offenders in vacation rentals)
flows.what: NGOs report tourists exploit children in Tangier in vacation rentals owned and managed by European nationals.

networks.name: Franco regime child removals and Spain's 'stolen babies'
networks.what: The Franco regime, Auxilio Social and the Women's Protection Board removed about 30,000 children of Republican prisoners and took babies of confined women into the early 1980s; later hospital 'stolen baby' cases reached the courts from 2011, with the first trial (Dr Eduardo Vela, 2018) ending in acquittal on limitation grounds.

networks.name: Welcome to Video
networks.what: Darknet video site paid in Bitcoin, about 1.2 million members; seized 2018. 337 arrests in 38 countries announced October 2019. Start year 2015 is not in the sources opened and is omitted from cases.

networks.name: Boylover forum
networks.what: 'Discussion-only' forum used to make contact before sharing abuse material privately; 670 suspects, 184 arrests, 230 children safeguarded (Operation Rescue, 2011).

networks.name: Kidflix
networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.

networks.name: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
networks.what: Not one organisation: thousands of local traffickers, often parents or relatives, paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse. IJM: 1 in 100 Filipino children affected in 2022.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

networks.name: Legion of Christ (Legionaries of Christ)
networks.what: Founded in Mexico in 1941 by Marcial Maciel. The Vatican said in 2010 that Maciel committed 'true crimes' and the Legion had shielded him, and placed it under a papal delegate. The Legion's December 2019 report acknowledged 175 minors abused 1941–2019, 60 by Maciel and the rest by 33 priests.

networks.name: Marist Brothers
networks.what: Teaching order founded in France. Listed 154 members accused in Australia (1980–2015); nine Brothers convicted in New Zealand; apologised for systemic abuse at Scottish schools; acknowledged at least 14 victims of one Brother in Chile; complaints against 12 teachers at Barcelona schools.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Tehuacán → Los Angeles → Mexico: Fr Nicolás Aguilar Rivera; Costa Rica → Mexico: Fr Mauricio Víquez (flight, extradited 2021).
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Jean Succar Kuri (Cancún): first report 2003, first action 2004 (1 years). Journalist Lydia Cacho, who exposed the ring and links to businessman Kamel Nacif, was arrested and harassed in 2005; Mexico's Supreme Court ruled 6-4 in 2007 that Puebla governor Mario Marín had no case to answer; Marín was arrested for her alleged torture only in 2021 Marcial Maciel (Legion of Christ): first report 1976, first action 2006 (30 years). Juan Vaca's 1976 letter reached the Vatican; formal charges filed 1998 were not pursued by the CDF
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. The middle of those waits is 12 years. In Rochdale in 1968, a pupil told the police about the local politician Cyril Smith and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2020: Mexican Episcopal Conference self-report, Jan 2020. 426 priests investigated over ten years, 217 removed; El Universal: only 6 of 156 alleged child abuse cases 2009-2019 ended in conviction
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. The research for this map found no national inquiry in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Casitas del Sur — children missing from church-run shelters; La Gran Familia ('Mamá Rosa') shelter raid, Zamora; Jean Succar Kuri — Cancún child sexual exploitation ring; Lydia Cacho's arrest — Puebla governor and businessman protected exploitation ring.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 238 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Jean Succar Kuri — Cancún child sexual exploitation ring
cases.who: Jean Succar Kuri (hotelier); associates named in Lydia Cacho's reporting
cases.what: Cancún hotel businessman Succar Kuri was detained in the United States (reported as Los Angeles/Arizona) in 2004 at the request of Mexico's federal prosecutors and Interpol, after complaints by several girls, and was later returned to Mexico. In 2011 a federal district court convicted him and sentenced him to 13 years; on appeal by both sides a Cancún appeals court raised the sentence to 112 years, which was upheld. In 2023 a federal circuit court annulled the 112-year sentence over procedural flaws and ordered a new ruling on sexual abuse and child pornography offences against seven minors, which reduced his term. He died in Cancún on 14 June 2024 while still serving his sentence. Journalist Lydia Cacho's book 'Los demonios del Edén' described him as the head of a child-exploitation network and linked him to Puebla businessman Kamel Nacif and Governor Mario Marín.
cases.cover_up: See the related record on journalist Lydia Cacho's 2005 arrest arranged after her book exposed the ring.

cases.title: Cartagena — 'La Madame' network exploiting girls for tourists (plea 2018)
cases.who: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ('La Madame')
cases.what: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ran a sex network from a Bocagrande apartment in Cartagena, supplying young women and minors to parties on yachts, in hotels and at beaches and sending women to Panama, Mexico, Miami and the Bahamas; prosecutors seized 15 ledgers of clients and payments, and a WhatsApp group listed 200 women. In 2018 she accepted charges of human trafficking and conspiracy in a plea deal and was sentenced to eight years and one month; she was released on parole in 2023. US ICE supported the investigation.
cases.cover_up: At hearings she threatened to reveal the names of politicians and powerful men she said were clients (her claim, unverified).

cases.title: Casitas del Sur — children missing from church-run shelters
cases.who: Iglesia Cristiana Restaurada (Restored Christian Church) shelters; Mexico City Attorney General's Office (PGJDF), which placed children there
cases.what: Children placed by Mexico City prosecutors in the private Casitas del Sur shelter, run by a church group, went missing. In October 2010 Mexico's federal Attorney General offered rewards for information on 14 children who disappeared in February 2009 from the Casitas del Sur shelter in Mexico City and from related homes in Nuevo Laredo and Quintana Roo, and about 5 million pesos for three people sought in the case, saying the children may have been taken by child traffickers. Earlier sources not re-checked for this map also cite the removal of 126 children by police and human rights staff on 29 January 2009 and obstruction charges against seven staff (not re-checked for this map).
cases.cover_up: A Mexico City legislator accused officials of the District Attorney's office of negligence and complicity, saying they warned the shelter of searches so children could be moved.

cases.title: La Gran Familia ('Mamá Rosa') shelter raid, Zamora
cases.who: La Gran Familia shelter, founded 1947 by Rosa del Carmen Verduzco ('Mamá Rosa')
cases.what: On 15 July 2014 the PGR's organised-crime unit (SEIDO) raided the shelter and freed 432 children and 138 adults living in squalid conditions; the PGR said some had suffered sexual abuse, and residents reported rape, being held for years, food deprivation and forced begging. The PGR ruled out charging the 79-year-old founder because of age and mental decline; six others faced charges from unlawful imprisonment to organised crime. The PGR also investigated claims that the shelter in effect bought children through notarised parental waivers. Verduzco died in 2018.
cases.cover_up: More than 40 complaints from parents had been filed with Michoacán's DIF and the federal Attorney General's Office (PGR) before the raid.

cases.title: Lydia Cacho's arrest — Puebla governor and businessman protected exploitation ring
cases.who: Mario Marín (Governor of Puebla); Kamel Nacif Borge (businessman)
cases.what: After journalist Lydia Cacho's book 'Los demonios del Edén' (2005) linked Cancún businessman Jean Succar Kuri's child-exploitation network to Puebla businessman Kamel Nacif and Puebla governor Mario Marín, Cacho was arrested in 2005 and says she was tortured. Arrest warrants for torture were issued against Marín and Nacif; Marín was arrested in Acapulco in February 2021, and Nacif was detained in Lebanon in May 2021 and later released there. Marín was moved to house arrest in August 2024, returned to prison in April 2025, and in July 2026 was again granted house arrest on health and age grounds while his trial for alleged torture of Cacho continues. Neither has been convicted; both are accused of torture, not of the abuse itself.
cases.cover_up: Intimidation of a journalist: after Cacho exposed the Cancún ring, Puebla police arrested her in Cancún and drove her about 900 miles to Puebla. Leaked calls (La Jornada, 14 Feb 2006) recorded Nacif and Marín discussing jailing her as a favour and having her abused in jail. Mexico's Supreme Court ruled 6–4 on 29 Nov 2007 that Marín had no case to answer.

cases.title: Carreto family — Tenancingo to New York trafficking
cases.who: Carreto family pimping network based in Tenancingo, Tlaxcala
cases.what: From 1991 to 2004 the Carreto family, based in San Miguel de Tenancingo, Tlaxcala, recruited young, poor women and girls in Mexico by deception and forced them into prostitution in brothels in Queens and Brooklyn, using rape, threats and forced abortion. Josue and Gerardo Flores Carreto were sentenced to 50 years each in April 2006 and Daniel Perez Alonso to 25 years. Their mother Consuelo Carreto Valencia was extradited in January 2007 and pleaded guilty to sex trafficking on 22 July 2008.

cases.title: Rendon-Reyes trafficking organization (Tenancingo)
cases.who: Rendon-Reyes Trafficking Organization, Tenancingo, Tlaxcala
cases.what: From December 2004 to November 2015 the Tenancingo-based Rendon-Reyes organization smuggled women and girls from Mexico and Central America into the US, forced them into prostitution and laundered proceeds back to Mexico. In January 2019 five members were sentenced in Brooklyn to between 15 and 25 years; others had pleaded guilty to racketeering and sex trafficking.

cases.title: Costa Rica — Fr Mauricio Víquez, convicted after fleeing to Mexico
cases.who: Archdiocese of San José; Episcopal Conference of Costa Rica
cases.what: Víquez, a former church spokesman on family issues, fled Costa Rica in 2018 when accusations surfaced, going via Panama to San Nicolás de los Garza, Mexico, where he was caught; he was extradited in 2021. The church expelled him from the clergy in 2019. In March 2022 he was sentenced to 20 years (6 for sexual abuse, 14 for rape) for abusing an 11-year-old boy in his parish in 2002–2003. In August 2022 a civil court ordered the archbishop and two church entities to pay about US$100,000 in damages.
cases.cover_up: A San José civil court ordered Archbishop José Rafael Quirós, the Episcopal Conference and the church's property entity to pay 65 million colones; the victims' lawyer said the church knew from 2002 and did nothing. Three other complaints were declared time-barred.

cases.title: NXIVM — Keith Raniere convicted (including sexual exploitation of a 15-year-old)
cases.who: NXIVM (self-help group run as a cult)
cases.what: A Brooklyn federal jury convicted NXIVM leader Keith Raniere in June 2019 of racketeering, racketeering conspiracy, sex trafficking, attempted sex trafficking, forced labour conspiracy and wire fraud conspiracy. Prosecutors proved as racketeering acts that at 45 he sexually exploited a 15-year-old girl and photographed the abuse. On 27 October 2020 he was sentenced to 120 years and fined $1.75 million.

cases.title: La Luz del Mundo — leader Naasón Joaquín García convicted
cases.who: La Luz del Mundo church (HQ Guadalajara, Mexico)
cases.what: Naasón Joaquín García, leader of La Luz del Mundo, was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport on 3 June 2019 on charges brought by the California Attorney General including forcible rape of a minor, production of child pornography and human trafficking. On 3 June 2022, days before trial, he pleaded guilty to three counts involving minors (two of forcible oral copulation and one lewd act on a 15-year-old), and on 8 June 2022 was sentenced to more than 16 years in prison. Co-defendant Alondra Ocampo pleaded guilty to four counts in 2020. In October 2023 a federal grand jury indicted him for producing and possessing child pornography involving a 16-year-old follower.

cases.title: Lev Tahor — leaders convicted of kidnapping children
cases.who: Lev Tahor (ultra-Orthodox sect)
cases.what: In December 2018 Lev Tahor leaders Nachman Helbrans and Mayer Rosner took a 14-year-old girl and her 12-year-old brother in the night from their mother's home in upstate New York and moved them through several states to Mexico, where the girl was returned to the adult man the group had 'married' her to religiously at 13. The mother had fled the group's Guatemala compound in November 2018 and been granted sole custody. Both children were recovered in Mexico after three weeks. A federal jury convicted the two men in November 2021, and on 31 March 2022 each was sentenced to 12 years. Founder Shlomo Helbrans had been convicted in New York in 1994 of kidnapping a 13-year-old boy.

cases.title: Mexico — bishops say 152 priests removed in nine years
cases.who: Mexican Episcopal Conference (CEM)
cases.what: On 10 February 2019 Archbishop Rogelio Cabrera of Monterrey, president of the Mexican Episcopal Conference, said 152 priests had been removed from ministry in the previous nine years after being found guilty of sexually abusing minors, some of whom were jailed. He said there was no exact figure for victims.
cases.cover_up: The CEM president said there was no national count of victims because 'each bishop handles these problems' and no central record exists.

cases.cover_up: Letters to the Vatican in 1976, 1978 and 1989 and formal charges in 1998 produced no action; Vatican in 2010 said the Legion had shielded Maciel; Maciel never laicised or tried

cases.title: Mexican bishops' conference — 426 priests investigated
cases.who: Conferencia del Episcopado Mexicano
cases.what: On 14 January 2020 the Mexican Episcopal Conference said it was investigating 426 priests over the previous ten years: 271 cases of abuse of minors in church settings and 155 other proceedings. It said 217 priests had been removed from their duties. El Universal reported in February 2020 that prosecutors had opened 156 investigations into such sexual offences by religious figures from 2009 to 2019, but four prosecutors' offices recorded only six sentences.
cases.cover_up: El Universal reported only six convictions out of 156 alleged abuse cases involving minors, 2009–2019

cases.title: Fr Nicolás Aguilar Rivera — Puebla diocese priest in Los Angeles
cases.who: Archdiocese of Los Angeles; Diocese of Tehuacán (Mexico)
cases.what: A visiting Mexican priest was assigned to two Los Angeles parishes in 1987. A 1988 police report says he abused 26 grade-school children between March 1987 and January 1988, many recruited as altar servers. A parent reported abuse to a pastor on 8 January 1988; he was removed the next day, charged with 19 felony counts of lewd acts on a child, but fled to Mexico before arrest. As of 2004 the case remained open.
cases.cover_up: Plaintiffs' attorneys produced a 1988 letter from the Bishop of Tehuacán saying he had warned Cardinal Mahony in 1987 about the priest; the archdiocese denied receiving the warning. The priest fled to Mexico after being relieved of duties and was never arrested.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)

patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. cases.title: Ukraine — rape and sexual violence by Russian forces incl. children (UN Commission of Inquiry)
cases.who: Russian armed forces and authorities
cases.what: The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine found that Russian authorities committed the war crimes of rape and other sexual violence; cases it investigated included a 16-year-old girl, and in September 2022 it said it had documented children raped, tortured and unlawfully confined. Ukraine's official Children of War platform records 23 children sexually abused, according to the Office of the Prosecutor General.

cases.what: The UN Secretary-General verified the abduction, beginning in 2022 and continuing into 2023, of 122 children (75 boys, 47 girls) attributed to Russian armed forces, affiliated armed groups and Russian authorities in occupied Ukrainian territories; 91 abductions by Russian armed forces had been verified for 2022. The 2025 report welcomed the reunification of two of these children and said the whereabouts of the rest remained unknown.

cases.title: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)
cases.who: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), Lebensborn e.V., SS
cases.what: Nazi Germany seized children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn and other homes and placed them with German families under new identities; DW reports estimates of up to 200,000 Polish children kidnapped and forcibly 'Germanized'. In the RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., Nuremberg Military Tribunal I), 14 leading officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, Lebensborn and related bodies were charged with crimes including the kidnapping of 'racially valuable' children; charges were read on 10 October 1947, the trial ran from 20 October 1947 to 17 February 1948, and on 10 March 1948 the tribunal convicted 13 — Greifelt was sentenced to life — and acquitted one.
cases.network: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA) and Lebensborn e.V.

cases.title: Russia — Dima Yakovlev Law bans adoption by US citizens
cases.who: Russian state
cases.what: On 28 December 2012 President Putin signed a law banning the adoption of Russian children by US families, effective 1 January 2013. It was named after Dima Yakovlev, a Russian toddler adopted by Americans who died in 2008 after being left for hours in a hot car; his adoptive father was found not guilty of involuntary manslaughter. The law was widely seen as retaliation for the US Magnitsky Act, signed on 14 December 2012. In 2010 a US adoptive mother had sent her 7-year-old adopted son alone on a one-way flight back to Russia, causing outrage. (This is a closure event, not a trafficking finding.)

cases.title: Ukraine — Ukrainian children given Russian citizenship and adopted into Russian families
cases.who: Russian state; Children's Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova
cases.what: On 30 May 2022 President Putin signed a decree easing Russian citizenship for Ukrainian children so they could be adopted by Russian families; Russia created a register of families wishing to adopt Ukrainian children and paid families per adopted child granted citizenship. Lvova-Belova said she had adopted a child from Mariupol herself. On 17 March 2023 the ICC issued arrest warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova for unlawful deportation and transfer of children. Yale HRL (14 February 2023) documented a 'systematic' programme of re-education and adoption. (Deportations and camps are recorded by the conflict agent; this record covers the adoption element.)

cases.title: Russia — deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children; ICC warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova
cases.who: Russian state: President Vladimir Putin; Children's Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova
cases.what: On 17 March 2023 ICC Pre-Trial Chamber II issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova for the war crimes of unlawful deportation and unlawful transfer of children from occupied Ukraine to Russia, committed from at least 24 February 2022. The UN Commission of Inquiry found a transfer of 31 children in May 2022 was unlawful deportation and a war crime; Lvova-Belova's own bulletin said 380 orphans had been placed with Russian foster families and about 2,000 children from institutions transferred in February 2022. Yale's Humanitarian Research Lab reported in February 2023 at least 43 camps in Russia and Crimea holding at least 6,000 Ukrainian children for 're-education'.

cases.title: Russia — 'Abandoned by the State': violence and neglect in orphanages for children with disabilities
cases.who: Russian state orphanages for children with disabilities
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's report of 15 September 2014, based on more than 200 interviews and visits to 10 state orphanages, found that many children with disabilities suffered serious abuse and neglect by staff, including beatings, sedative injections and being sent to psychiatric hospitals as punishment. Children deemed most severely disabled were confined to cribs in 'lying-down rooms', often tied to furniture. The report did not centre on sexual abuse; it is recorded here as institutional abuse and removal of children from families.
cases.cover_up: Children had few if any meaningful ways to seek help or report abuse; health workers pressured parents to give up disabled children.

cases.title: Kosovo — trafficking for forced prostitution and the international presence (Amnesty 2004)
cases.who: Criminal networks; demand from NATO KFOR soldiers, UN police and international staff
cases.what: Amnesty International's May 2004 report said Kosovo had become a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution since NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in 1999, with the international presence generating 80% of traffickers' income at the time. Women and girls were brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia via Serbia, and local girls were also abducted. The UN peacekeeping department acknowledged in 2004 that peacekeepers had 'come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution'.
cases.cover_up: Amnesty found no evidence of criminal proceedings against any military personnel in their home countries.

cases.title: France charges Telegram founder Pavel Durov
cases.who: Telegram (messaging platform)
cases.what: Durov was arrested at Le Bourget airport on 24 August 2024 and on 28 August a Paris investigating judge placed him under formal investigation on all the charges for which he was arrested, including suspected complicity in running a platform allowing illicit transactions, images of child sexual abuse, drug trafficking and fraud, and refusal to communicate information to authorities. He was released on 5 million euros bail, required to report to police twice a week and barred from leaving France. A BBC investigation that month found Telegram was not a member of NCMEC or the IWF and had ignored repeated requests to join. On 4 December 2024 the IWF announced Telegram would use its hashes of known abuse images to detect such material in public parts of the platform; the IWF said it had confirmed thousands of reports of abuse imagery on Telegram since 2022.

cases.title: Blue Orchid — Russian site selling abuse videos
cases.who: Blue Orchid website
cases.what: A Moscow-based website that sold videotapes of the sexual abuse of boys, some as young as 12, for $200 to $300 each, mostly mailed to customers in the United States. The investigation began in May 2000 when Moscow police asked the US Customs Service for help; Russian police arrested the alleged operators in December 2000 and the site was shut in January 2001. By 26 March 2001 US Customs announced that four US citizens and five Russians had been arrested, with customers arrested in California, New York and Indiana and leads passed to Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands.

cases.title: Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan — girls lured to cities; children in institutions (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers recruiting via social media
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers lure girls and women from rural Kazakhstan and neighbouring Central Asian, East Asian and Eastern European countries with job offers as waitresses, models or nannies in large cities, and exploit Kazakh women and girls in Russia, Uzbekistan, the Middle East, Europe, East Asia and the US. In Uzbekistan, children in institutions are vulnerable to sex trafficking.

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. cases.title: Norway — state investigation of illegal intercountry adoptions (2023–)
cases.who: Norwegian state; private adoption organisations
cases.what: Norway launched an investigation in 2023 into whether illegal or unethical practices occurred in intercountry adoptions and whether Norwegian officials failed to control them; the foreign ministry said it was 'aware of serious findings' (AP, 2024). Norway received 6,295 Korean children 1955–2008, and in 1974–75 Scandinavian diplomats pressed South Korea to keep sending children after it tried to stop. In September 2025 a Korean-born adoptee served notice of a lawsuit against the Norwegian state alleging her adoption was illegal (allegation).

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Thorbjørn Jagland — charged with aggravated corruption over Epstein ties
cases.who: Thorbjørn Jagland (former Norwegian PM, Council of Europe Secretary General, Nobel Committee chair)
cases.what: After the US Justice Department's 2026 release of Epstein documents, Norway's economic-crime agency Økokrim opened an investigation into former prime minister and Council of Europe secretary-general Thorbjørn Jagland on suspicion of aggravated corruption, looking into 'whether gifts, travel and loans were received in connection with his position'. On 12 Feb 2026 his lawyers said he had been charged with aggravated corruption; his Oslo home and two other properties were searched. He denies all charges. This is a corruption case, not an abuse charge; recorded for the network's political reach.

cases.title: Norwegian children's homes and special schools 1945–1980 (NOU 2004:23)
cases.who: Norwegian municipal children's homes and state special schools
cases.what: The official report NOU 2004:23 'Barnehjem og spesialskoler under lupen' found neglect and abuse, in part of a serious nature and including sexual abuse, in children's homes and special schools between 1945 and 1980. Bergen and other municipalities ran their own investigations and compensation schemes; in 2005 the Storting committee recommended adapting the state 'rettferdsvederlag' scheme with payments up to NOK 300,000 and a lower burden of proof.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

cases.title: Project COMPASS against 'The Com' network

cases.what: Coordinated by Europol's European Counter Terrorism Centre with EU states, Norway, Switzerland, the UK, US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand (28 countries). Since January 2025 it has contributed to 30 arrests, 179 identified or partially identified perpetrators, 62 identified or partially identified victims and 4 victims safeguarded. The FBI warned the public about The Com on 23 July 2025.

cases.who: Buyers paying cryptocurrency for dark web forum access
cases.what: From late May to mid-June 2026 police in Canada, Czechia, Germany, Norway, Poland, Sweden and Switzerland arrested 28 men aged 22–54 suspected of paying cryptocurrency to access dark web forums with abuse videos; one used AI to generate material and some victims were family members. Norwegian police used a crypto-tracing method developed in 2025, which also identified two sellers.

cases.what: From 24 to 28 June 2024, 32 investigators at Europol processed leads from US HSI investigations into networks exploiting children in the Philippines: over 10 million lines of chat between about 12,000 customer accounts and 100 seller accounts, built up over 12 years. The sprint produced information packages that may lead authorities in 24 countries to 197 buyers. Europol notes buyers direct traffickers to abuse children in real time on webcam and some travel to the Philippines to abuse children in person.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found South Asia lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
cases.what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

cases.title: MINUSTAH Sri Lankan contingent — child sexual exploitation ring, Haiti
cases.who: Sri Lanka Army contingent of the UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti (MINUSTAH)
cases.what: In November 2007, 114 members of the 950-strong Sri Lankan contingent were accused of sexual misconduct and abuse, and 108, including three officers, were sent home. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services concluded that 'acts of sexual exploitation and abuse (against children) were frequent and occurred usually at night, and at virtually every location where the contingent personnel were deployed', and said charges should include statutory rape. An Associated Press investigation in April 2017 found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had exploited at least nine children in a sex ring between 2004 and 2007; none was jailed.
cases.cover_up: Repatriation instead of prosecution: 114 Sri Lankan peacekeepers were sent home; Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts 'consensual' and nobody was jailed.
cases.network: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)

cases.title: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
cases.who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cases.what: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.
cases.cover_up: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.

cases.title: Switzerland — authorities' irregularities in intercountry adoptions (Sri Lanka, India, Tibet…); proposed ban
cases.who: Swiss federal and cantonal authorities; private adoption agencies
cases.what: Swiss authorities soon realised that the placement of children for adoption, often wrongly presented as orphans, was also driven by economic interests and linked to organised child trafficking; decisions were often made on incomplete or falsified documents, and checks on foster families and on legal requirements were insufficient. From the 2010s, under pressure from groups such as Back to the Roots, intercountry adoptions from Tibet, Sri Lanka and India drew public attention. In 2018 the Federal Assembly commissioned a study on intercountry adoption; the Federal Council acknowledged the authorities' irregularities and omissions in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 recommended a general ban on intercountry adoption.

cases.title: Seth Sevana children's home, Vavuniya — monk arrested, bail with NCPA consent
cases.who: Seth Sevana Lama Nivasa children's home (run by a Buddhist monk) housing war-affected Tamil children; National Child Protection Authority (NCPA)
cases.what: In October 2013 the head of a children's home in Vavuniya, a Buddhist monk, was arrested for sexually abusing a 9-year-old child, confirmed by medical evidence on 12 October 2013. The NCPA took custody of the other 22 children on 15 October 2013. Most children were war-affected Tamil children placed by poor families. Groundviews reported that complaints had reached the NCPA since 2010 and that the agency later supported his release on bail.
cases.cover_up: Complaints had been made to the NCPA since 2010; the arrest came only after protests by Vavuniya child protection officers. On 31 December 2013 the monk got unconditional bail after the Attorney General's Department, on NCPA instructions, told the court it had no objection; the NCPA did not submit the 22 children's reports to the court.

cases.title: Anuradhapura children's home — probation officials arrested
cases.who: North Central Provincial Department of Probation and Child Care Services
cases.what: After a media report on 8 January 2021 of illegal activity at a children's home near Anuradhapura and a complaint by the National Child Protection Authority on 16 January 2021, police arrested a former provincial Commissioner and a Senior Probation Officer of the Department of Probation and Child Care Services. They were accused over the treatment of a 17-year-old girl held at a counselling centre on court orders who was made to work as a cook in a children's home. They were granted bail by the Anuradhapura Magistrate's Court and the Attorney General's advice was sought on further action.

cases.title: Sri Lanka — child sex tourism in coastal areas (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Foreign and local offenders
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers reportedly exploit boys and girls in child sex trafficking, including in coastal areas, for foreign offenders, and recommends investigating complicit establishments. The government convicted six traffickers and identified seven child victims in the year.

networks.name: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
networks.what: UN Secretary-General reports record 357 SEA allegations against peacekeeping personnel in 2006, falling to 51 in 2014 and rising to 102 in 2024. In 2024, 27 of 125 identified victims were children. Most allegations since 2018 come from MONUSCO (DRC) and MINUSCA (CAR). Criminal accountability rests with troop-contributing countries; the UN can only repatriate.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2010: Independent Victims' Protection Commission (Klasnic Commission), set up by bishops spring 2010. Set a four-tier compensation model (EUR 5,000 / 15,000 / 25,000 / more in extreme cases)
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. The research for this map found no national inquiry in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Wilhelminenberg children's home, Vienna — commission report
cases.who: City of Vienna children's home at Wilhelminenberg
cases.what: A commission set up by the City of Vienna presented a 344-page report on 12 June 2013, based on 217 interviews including 140 former residents. It found children at the city-run home (1948–1977, girls only from 1962) were rampantly abused, including rape and sexual exploitation by caregivers and outside men, with girls as young as about six. Findings were sent to prosecutors. Some former residents received payments of up to €35,000.
cases.cover_up: Municipal staff in the overseeing department knew of widespread abuse and did not act; city politicians who learned of it in the 1960s also ignored it.

cases.title: Romania — girls in state institutions at risk; victims sent across Europe (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers; staff of some government-run institutions
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says most identified victims are women and girls exploited in Romania and in Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK; children in government-run institutions, particularly girls in homes for persons with disabilities, are at risk of sex trafficking; and Roma children as young as 11 are 'sold' into marriage. Courts convicted 161 traffickers (143 for sex trafficking) and 600 victims were identified in 2024.
cases.cover_up: Alleged complicity, misconduct and negligence by government employees in cases involving children in government-run homes remained a concern.

cases.title: Elysium darknet platform
cases.who: Elysium (darknet forum and chats, over 87,000 members)
cases.what: Elysium existed from late 2016 and was used to exchange abuse material and to arrange the sexual abuse of children; it had German, French, Spanish and Italian chat groups. German prosecutors (ZIT Frankfurt) and the BKA shut it down in June 2017 after Australian police passed on a lead; 14 suspects were arrested, 12 suspected of abusing children themselves. On 7 March 2019 the Limburg court sentenced four men to between 3 years 10 months and 9 years 9 months, with preventive detention for the main administrator.

cases.title: Bergisch Gladbach abuse complex
cases.who: Chat groups of men sharing recordings of abuse of their own and other children
cases.what: In October 2019 police found a large cache of child abuse images and videos at a house in Bergisch Gladbach; the man there had repeatedly abused his daughter, born in 2017, and shared recordings in chat groups. On 6 October 2020 Cologne Regional Court sentenced him to 12 years plus preventive detention. Investigators found more than 30,000 pseudonyms used in the network, many untraceable; by January 2022 Cologne police had identified 439 suspects, secured numerous convictions and rescued 65 children aged from three months to 17. Two other men, from Krefeld and Viersen, were sentenced to 14.5 and 13.5 years.
cases.network: North Rhine-Westphalia abuse complexes (Lügde, Bergisch Gladbach)

cases.title: Cardinal Groër affair and Klasnic victims' commission, Austria
cases.who: Archdiocese of Vienna; Austrian Bishops' Conference; Independent Victims' Protection Commission (Klasnic Commission)
cases.what: Archbishop of Vienna Cardinal Hans Hermann Groër stepped down in September 1995 after a former pupil, followed by others, accused him of sexual abuse; in 1998 Austrian bishops said they considered the allegations well founded, and the Holy See opened an inquiry. In spring 2010 the bishops set up the Independent Victims' Protection Commission chaired by Waltraud Klasnic. By 31 August 2021, according to the church's victims' foundation, payments had been approved in 2,550 cases, about €33 million in total. At Kremsmünster Abbey, the former head of the boarding school was jailed for 12 years in 2013 for crimes against 24 former pupils, 15 of them victims of sexual abuse.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

cases.title: Austria-led 2007 investigation — 2,360 suspects in 77 countries
cases.who: Online distribution network uncovered by Austrian authorities
cases.what: The investigation began in July 2006 when an employee of a Vienna-based file-hosting service reported suspicious material; within 24 hours investigators recorded more than 8,000 hits from 2,361 IP addresses in 77 countries. On 7 February 2007 Austrian authorities announced more than 2,360 suspects who had paid to view videos of young children being sexually abused; the FBI was investigating about 600, about 130 were Australian, France was looking at about 100 and at least 23 were Austrian. Germany had the largest number of suspects. No suspects were yet in custody at the announcement.
cases.cover_up: The two Irish suspects were not investigated by the Garda until six months after Austria notified them.

cases.title: New Zealand DIA-led operation: 146 children safeguarded
cases.who: Tens of thousands of accounts sharing abuse material on an online service
cases.what: Begun in 2019 after an online service provider reported offenders exchanging imagery of the sadistic abuse of infants and children. By March 2022 it had opened 836 cases internationally, led to 46 arrests across New Zealand, identified more than 100 suspects in the EU and safeguarded 146 children; in Austria and Hungary suspects were abusing their own children.

cases.title: Europol sprint on buyers of live-distant abuse in the Philippines (2024)
cases.who: Buyers worldwide directing livestreamed abuse by traffickers in the Philippines
cases.what: From 24 to 28 June 2024, 32 investigators at Europol processed leads from US HSI investigations into networks exploiting children in the Philippines: over 10 million lines of chat between about 12,000 customer accounts and 100 seller accounts, built up over 12 years. The sprint produced information packages that may lead authorities in 24 countries to 197 buyers. Europol notes buyers direct traffickers to abuse children in real time on webcam and some travel to the Philippines to abuse children in person.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 24,212 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman). 2007: scandal + law: Casa Quivira raid (August, 46 children); Hague-compliant adoption law passed 11 December 2007 2008: closure: Guatemala stops new adoptions to the US from 1 January; US State Dept (9 January) says no new US adoptions until Hague-compliant 2010: report: CICIG report on illegal adoption finds 78% of 153 cases studied violated the law
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: Guatemala — notary-run adoption trade to the US (1996–2007).
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, about 500 babies were taken from mothers held in detention and given to other families; in 2012 a court found this had been a "systematic plan", and by July 2025, 140 of those children had been identified. Under Franco's dictatorship in Spain, children were taken from Republican mothers and later from unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children from their families and placed them in residential schools or with non-Indigenous families. In 1951 Denmark sent a group of Greenlandic children to live with Danish families, and France moved children from the island of Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported children from occupied parts of Ukraine; in March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over these deportations.

cases.title: Guatemala — notary-run adoption trade to the US (1996–2007)
cases.who: Private notaries (notarios), baby brokers, foster homes, officials
cases.what: After the civil war ended in 1996, adoptions abroad rose each year, run almost entirely (about 98%) by private notaries who handled both sides without court review and charged $35,000 or more per child; 97% of children went to the US. CICIG's 2010 report studied 153 cases and found 78% violated the new law in some way. Guatemala passed a Hague-compliant law on 11 December 2007 and stopped new adoptions to the US from 1 January 2008; the US State Department announced on 9 January 2008 it would not allow new adoptions until procedures were compliant.

cases.title: Hogar Seguro Virgen de la Asunción — abuse, trafficking alerts and fire killing 41 girls
cases.who: State-run children's home under the Secretariat of Social Welfare (SBS); National Civil Police
cases.what: About 700 children lived at the state home, built for a maximum of 500; most had committed no crime. Months before the fire prosecutors had recommended closing it over abuse allegations, and girls had protested overcrowding and alleged sexual abuse by staff. After an escape on 7 March 2017, police returned a group of girls and locked them in a room; on 8 March one girl set a mattress alight, killing 41 girls and injuring 15. The social welfare secretary, his deputy and the home's director were sacked and later charged. On 12 Aug 2025 a judge convicted six former officials of offences from manslaughter to abuse of authority, with sentences of 6 to 25 years; former secretary Carlos Rodas received 25 years and a police officer who held the key 13 years. The judge said the fire was the culmination of reported abuses not acted on, and ordered an investigation of former President Jimmy Morales.
cases.cover_up: Officials ignored repeated complaints: in November 2016 the Human Rights Ombudsman asked the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights for precautionary measures citing mistreatment and a trafficking network recruiting children from the home. On the day of the fire police guarding the locked room did not let the girls out.

cases.title: Rendon-Reyes trafficking organization (Tenancingo)
cases.who: Rendon-Reyes Trafficking Organization, Tenancingo, Tlaxcala
cases.what: From December 2004 to November 2015 the Tenancingo-based Rendon-Reyes organization smuggled women and girls from Mexico and Central America into the US, forced them into prostitution and laundered proceeds back to Mexico. In January 2019 five members were sentenced in Brooklyn to between 15 and 25 years; others had pleaded guilty to racketeering and sex trafficking.

cases.title: Lev Tahor — leaders convicted of kidnapping children
cases.who: Lev Tahor (ultra-Orthodox sect)
cases.what: In December 2018 Lev Tahor leaders Nachman Helbrans and Mayer Rosner took a 14-year-old girl and her 12-year-old brother in the night from their mother's home in upstate New York and moved them through several states to Mexico, where the girl was returned to the adult man the group had 'married' her to religiously at 13. The mother had fled the group's Guatemala compound in November 2018 and been granted sole custody. Both children were recovered in Mexico after three weeks. A federal jury convicted the two men in November 2021, and on 31 March 2022 each was sentenced to 12 years. Founder Shlomo Helbrans had been convicted in New York in 1994 of kidnapping a 13-year-old boy.

cases.title: Guatemala — Casa Quivira raid: 46 children possibly stolen for adoption
cases.who: Casa Quivira private adoption home (run by a US citizen and his Guatemalan wife); two lawyers
cases.what: On 11 August 2007 Guatemalan police found 46 children aged a few days to three years at the Casa Quivira adoption home in Antigua after neighbours reported foreigners collecting children daily. Two lawyers who allegedly processed the adoptions were arrested. Attorney General Mario Gordillo said most of the children lacked proper documents and his office was investigating whether they had been stolen or obtained from mothers under coercion.

cases.title: Honduras, El Salvador, Guatemala — gangs exploit girls; North American offenders (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Gangs and criminal organizations; foreign offenders
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP reports say criminal organizations including gangs exploit girls in sex trafficking in urban Honduras and Guatemala, and that men from Canada and the US exploit Honduran children. In El Salvador, foreign tourists sexually exploit children and the rapid growth of tourism has created new risks; an estimated 140,000–200,000 Salvadoran children have a parent abroad or detained. Guatemalan children are exploited in Mexico and the US and in live-streamed abuse.

cases.title: Lev Tahor — Guatemala removal of 160 minors
cases.who: Lev Tahor
cases.what: In December 2024 Guatemalan authorities removed 160 children from a Lev Tahor property in Oratorio, Santa Rosa, where the group had settled in 2016, after four minors escaped and reported abuse; the group was accused of sexual violence against minors and human trafficking. Members later forced their way into a shelter and tried to take back children. The group had earlier left the United States and Canada for Mexico and Guatemala.

flows.what: US immigrant visas issued to children adopted from Guatemala, FY1994–FY2014 (peak 4,728 in FY2007).

flows.title: Guatemala / Honduras → Mexico → United States (children in sex trafficking)
flows.what: Guatemalan and Honduran adults and children exploited in sex trafficking in Mexico, the US, Belize and El Salvador.

flows.title: Chatham-Kent, Ontario → Guatemala (Lev Tahor flees child-protection orders)
flows.what: After a Quebec court ordered 14 children into foster care in November 2013 and the group moved to Ontario, members with children left for Guatemala in 2014; nine who tried to flee via Trinidad and Tobago were returned to Canada.

networks.name: Tenancingo (Tlaxcala) pimping family networks
networks.what: Family-based pimping networks from Tenancingo, Tlaxcala, that recruited Mexican and Central American women and girls by deception and forced them into prostitution in New York and other US cities. Several were prosecuted in Brooklyn (Carreto family, 2005–2008; Rendon-Reyes organization, 2019).

networks.name: Lev Tahor
networks.what: Ultra-Orthodox sect of about 200–300 people founded in Israel in 1988 by Shlomo Helbrans, accused of child abuse and forced marriage of teenage girls. Leaders were convicted in the US in 2021 of kidnapping two children.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Lima → Bolivia: Jesuit Alfonso Pedrajas; Chile → Peru: Marist Brother Abel Pérez.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.role_note: 9,941 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (3% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

cases.title: Kosovo — trafficking for forced prostitution and the international presence (Amnesty 2004)
